question: In Wilson disease presenting as fulminant hepatic failure, serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is paradoxically LOW or normal, despite severe liver injury — this pattern, combined with Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia, is a diagnostic clue to Wilson disease.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is TRUE. In most liver diseases, ALP rises with jaundice. Wilson disease FHF is the exception: ALP is paradoxically LOW or normal. This occurs because the massive copper release causes a Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia that destroys the zinc-containing ALP enzyme. The combination of FHF + low ALP + haemolysis = Wilson disease until proven otherwise. Slit-lamp for Kayser-Fleischer rings and 24-h urine copper confirm the diagnosis.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Wilson disease FHF has a pathognomonic biochemical paradox: ALP is LOW (often <40 U/L) despite gross hyperbilirubinaemia and encephalopathy, because massive hepatic copper release causes haemolysis (consuming zinc-dependent ALP) and Kayser-Fleischer rings may be visible on slit-lamp. Treatment for Wilson disease outside FHF = D-penicillamine or trientine + zinc. In FHF, urgent liver transplantation is often the only option as the copper load cannot be chelated fast enough.
